Stated Claim / Post Context:
LIVE: Election night updates

Stick with Richmonder.org all night for the latest.

Actual Article Body:
Completing registration...

Something's gone wrong. Please try again.

Success! Check your inbox for our email.

Stick with Richmonder.org all night for the latest. New updates will be added to the top of this page.

10:16 p.m. – An absolute stunner in the 6th District school board race. With 7 of the 8 precincts reporting their in-person vote, it appears that Jackie McDonnough will defeat Anne Holton for the seat.

McDonnough has 3,332 votes to Holton's 1,436. VPAP says there are about 3,000 early votes remaining to be counted, but it would take a massive surprise for Holton to overcome the margin.

This is potentially the biggest upset to come out of election night. We'll have plenty more as the evening goes on.

10:04 p.m. – Chesterfield's school board race is in the books, and as expected, Christina Brady will win the vacant seat in the Clover Hill district.

9:47 p.m. – It's a wild one in Chesterfield.

Most of the early vote has been counted, and with 158,526 votes tallied from the county, the sales tax increase is currently failing by a 613-vote margin.

Stay tuned. There may be much more to come on that one.

Meanwhile, we're still waiting for more of the Richmond vote to roll in, but we've seen nothing to suggest that the sales tax increase won't pass easily in the city.

8:45 p.m. – Not much action to report on in the 8 p.m. hour. We've now seen all of Chesterfield's day-of vote, which is leaning very slightly "no" on the sales tax increase. However, more people early voted in Chesterfield than voted day-of, so there's plenty of time for that to reverse. It's far too early to call, with "yes" being in a slightly better position at the moment.

There's a clear rural/urban split in the county, with the more urban (closer to Richmond) voters trending yes on the increase.

In Richmond, we've seen part of one precinct's vote in the Anne Holton-Jackie McDonnough school board race, and it's a big margin for McDonnough. There's just no way to extrapolate off those numbers, so it'll have to remain a curiosity for the moment.

Richmond's "Yes for RPS" campaign appears to be getting the job done, though. If we were in the prediction game, we'd be awfully close to making the call.

8:06 p.m. – Catch video updates from the newsroom all night long on Instagram at RichmonderNews

7:54 p.m. – An early surprise out of Chesterfield, which was considered likely to pass the 1% sales tax increase easily, as residents did with a bond referendum four years ago.

Unlike Richmond, the "no" vote has a strong early showing in Chesterfield. That said, keep in mind that we are only looking at day-of vote, and we have not seen any of the early vote yet, which is likely to be a larger overall number than the day-of vote.

There's still plenty of time for this number to swing, but as "yes" solidifies in Richmond, it's much more uncertain in Chesterfield.

7:28 p.m. – We've got our first two precincts reporting in Richmond, and it's good news for the "Yes for RPS" campaign, though there's still a ways to go.

These are both 1st District sites in the Near West End, where you'd expect cynicism about the 1% sales tax to be at its highest.

Still a long ways to go, but the very first indicator is positive for a potential sales tax increase.

5:50 p.m. – Polls close in a little more than one hour in Richmond, and turnout appears to be high on a beautiful day across the region.

Early voting numbers came in strong as well, with Chesterfield, Henrico and Richmond residents participating in early voting at 6-12% higher rates than they did in last year's elections.

Here are some of the things we'll be watching as the results begin coming in:

Expect plenty more, as well as video updates and chats with voters, as we settle in at Richmonder HQ to document what promises to be an eventful night.

Live 2026 Election updates: Results could be delayed until 9 p.m. due to long lines across Utah

Today’s the day: Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. as Utah voters help decide on elected officials to represent them everywhere from their local county building to Washington, D.C.

Actual Article Body:
(Abigail Landwehr  |  The Salt Lake Tribune) People wait in line to vote at Salt Lake City Public Library in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

Comment

Add as Preferred Source

Long lines across Utah are delaying election results. The state’s elections results website noted that lines are longer than 15 minutes and that “results will be delayed until lines are less than 15 minutes anywhere in the state, but no later than 9 p.m.”

At 8:07 p.m., there were a few hundred voters in line at the Cache County Event Center, but the line was moving steadily. County Clerk Bryson Behm estimated it would take about an hour to get everyone through.

Polls have closed in Utah’s elections, but if you’re in line you can still vote! Voters in line as of 8 p.m. have the right to cast a ballot.

Once all voters have cast their ballots, officials expect to start releasing early election results. Stay up to date on those races at sltrib.com/politics/election/

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

About 10 minutes before polls closed, about 50 people were in line outside the Salt Lake City Main Library, with more walking up to join the line.

Farther south, at the Draper Recreation Center, there were no lines to be seen with 10 minutes to go until 8 p.m.

In Utah County, voters lined up in their cars outside the American Fork Library to drop off their ballots.

Hours earlier in Cache County, voters were streaming through the county’s event center to cast their ballots.

Voter Douglas Goldman, who said his main priority was to keep government small, was frustrated at having to show his ID several times during the in-person voting process.

Roman Metivier, on the other hand, thought things were running smoothly. He had voted a few days earlier, but was at the center with several of his family members who were also there to cast ballots.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune) An election monitor who works for the Department of Justice observes voting at Herriman City Hall on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

In St. George, voters faced lengthy lines at the Dixie Convention Center Tuesday evening, with some waiting over an hour to cast their ballot.

Crystal Hanza, who voted early, waited patiently in line with her two daughters who are students at Utah Tech University.

Despite the long lines, Roxy Hanza, 21, said the voting process went smoothly and she appreciated all the volunteers.

“Everyone was nice in there, and I think as a young person, it’s important that we go and vote,” she said.

She saw some of her classmates in line too, she added, and has seen young people posting about the election on social media.

Immigration and other social issues influenced the Hanzas’ votes this year.

She held up a rainbow charm on her necklace and told The Tribune she wore it in memory of Renee Good, who was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Minneapolis.

(Brooke Larsen | The Salt Lake Tribune) Voters stand in line at the Dixie Convention Center in St. George on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

“I do understand we need to have safe borders,” she added, “but I don’t think we need to be dehumanizing and ruthless about it.”

Jeremy Bradley told The Tribune he thought a lot of Washington County voters were turning out because of frustration with Utah judges. “I’ve had some friends say just vote no on all the judges, out with the old in with the new,” he said, “but I did not vote that way.”

For Navajo voters, Tuesday is a double Election Day.

“Not only do we have the county, state and federal races, we also have the Navajo Nation elections,” said Carma Claw, president of the Aneth Chapter in the Utah portion of the Navajo Nation.

Waves of floods have devastated the Navajo Nation and eroded dirt roads, cutting off access to polling locations for some. It’s why the state is allowing San Juan County residents to vote electronically.

But not all tribal members have internet access, Claw said, and the Navajo Nation doesn’t have an electronic voting option.

“Some are just saying they don’t have an ability to get here because of road closures,” Claw said. “There’s been a lot of areas in the community where the regular dirt roads are washed out completely.”

(Navajo Nation Division of Transportation) Heavy rains washed out Flat Top Mountain Road in Red Mesa, forcing a route closure on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, two days before Election Day.

Poll workers had to navigate eroded roads early Tuesday to setup voting centers, said Claw, who thanked poll workers, election staff and volunteers “for making voting even an option given this flood damage.”

Aneth Chapter members have to go two locations — 8 miles apart — to participate in both the U.S. election and Navajo Nation election. One voter told Claw they had to take a two-hour-long detour.

The San Juan River is expected to rise again Tuesday night, which could make the road between both locations “impassable,” Claw said.

Moving forward, the experience may inform organizers on how to better prepare for elections during natural disasters.

“This is a really important opportunity for people to voice their input, and a natural disaster should not be a part of why they can’t have that access,” Claw added.

Federal election monitors have stopped by at least half of Salt Lake County’s 40 voting centers, Chief Deputy Clerk Nikila Venugopal said Tuesday afternoon.

Turnout has remained steady throughout the day, Venugopal said, with voters quickly moving through the lines to drop off their ballots.

So far, neither Venugopal nor Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman were aware of any problems involving the federal monitors.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune) Three election monitors who identified themselves as working for the Department of Justice observe voting at Herriman City Hall on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune) Voters cast their ballots at Midvale City Hall on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune) Voters at Midvale City Hall on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

In Davis County, Clerk Brian McKenzie said Election Day voting had been “going really well,” with a steady stream of voters, both in-person and at drop boxes.

He expects that somewhere around 40-50% of voters — typical turnout for a midterm election — would cast ballots before polls close at 8 p.m.

Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman said federal election monitors sent by President Donald Trump’s Justice Department are visiting all 40 voting centers in the county Tuesday, spending about 30 minutes at each site.

By about noon, monitors had already hit several polling locations, including the Salt Lake County Government Center on State Street and Unified Fire Authority’s Fire Station 123 in Herriman, she said.

So far, Chapman said the monitors have followed state election laws and have not interacted with voters or disrupted the voting process.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune)  A voter at Draper Recreation Center on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

A spokesperson for Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson’s office also said Tuesday morning that they had not heard of any issues. The monitors were only expected in Salt Lake County.

Throughout the county, Salt Lake Tribune staff are seeing polling locations with steady but manageable lines.

At the Draper Recreation Center, at 657 E. Vestry Rd., polling staff said they saw long lines when it first opened at 7 a.m. — mostly from sweaty patrons looking to cast their vote after their morning workout. But by early afternoon, lines had shrunken considerably.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune)  Voting takes place in the Council Chambers at Draper City Hall on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

The estimated preelection turnout from Utah voters before polls opened throughout the state early Tuesday was 30%, Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson announced.

The highest turnout was in Grand County, with 60% estimated turnout, followed by Rich County with 58.8%.

In Utah County, where Clerk Aaron Davidson has said he is a proponent of in-person voting, preelection turnout was 19.3%, the second-lowest in the state. In Salt Lake County, the number hovered just under 34%.

On Tuesday morning, around 9 a.m., a steady stream of voters lined up at the ballot drop box outside the downtown Salt Lake City library — and found it nearly stuffed to the top. An elections division worker with the Salt Lake County clerk’s office noted someone was on the way to retrieve ballots as people continued to vote.

(Rachel Crosby | The Salt Lake Tribune) A driver votes across from City Hall in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

About 2.5 miles south, at the Salt Lake County Government Center, a Salt Lake Tribune reporter also noted cars queuing for the location’s drive-thru ballot drop box.

There were also plenty of residents walking inside to vote in-person.

Some San Juan County residents woke up to an email offering them an unusual option Tuesday, after flooding prompted Utah’s top election official to allow affected voters to cast their ballots electronically.

Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson declared emergency election accommodations Monday as record rainfall and flooding continued to disrupt the county, blocking roads and making it difficult for some residents to reach ballot drop boxes and polling locations.

“We want to make sure that every voter knows that they’re important, that their vote matters, and that if they wish to do so, they have every opportunity to cast their vote,” Henderson said at a news conference Monday.

San Juan County has about 6,000 registered voters, Henderson said, and the county clerk’s office has limited staff and is already “spread really thin.”

Unlocking the electronic option is a temporary emergency measure and will not change the state’s regular voting process in the future, she said.

The county sent an email Tuesday morning to voters who may need the accommodation and have an email address on file. Residents who have not voted and did not receive an email can contact the county clerk before 5 p.m. All electronic ballots must be submitted by 8 p.m.

County officials declared a local emergency Sunday, and Bluff Mayor Josh Ewing described the latest round of rain as “a one-two punch.”

Henderson, making her second visit to the county in a week, said Monday that roads and bridges had been washed away or submerged, while some homes and businesses were destroyed. Communities were just beginning to recover from last week’s flooding when more rain fell on already saturated ground over the weekend.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune) The voting location at Riverton City Hall on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

Today’s the day! Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. as Utah voters decide on who will represent them in offices everywhere from their local county government to Washington, D.C.

More than 1.7 million Utahns are registered to vote, according to Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson’s office.

Henderson, who oversees statewide elections, said about a third of voters had cast ballots as of Monday morning, with turnout ranging from 18% in San Juan County to more than 45% in Rich and Grand counties.

Three members of Utah’s House delegation are up for reelection, as U.S. Reps. Blake Moore, Celeste Maloy and Mike Kennedy look to win again in newly drawn congressional districts. U.S. Rep. Burgess Owens, who currently represents the state’s 4th Congressional District, is retiring, while former U.S. Rep. Ben McAdams is running again in the new 1st Congressional District.

Utahns also will vote for members of the state Legislature, two proposed congressional amendments, county councils, school boards and whether to retain judges.

Want to learn more about the races on your ballot? Check out The Tribune’s voter guides. Plug in your address and find guides for every race on your ballot.

In past elections, ballots postmarked on or by Election Day would be counted. But a change to Utah’s election laws now requires filled-out ballots to be in the hands of election officials or in an official drop box by 8 p.m. on election night to be counted.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune)  Voting takes place at the Sandy Library on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

That means it’s far too late to mail your ballot, but there are still plenty of ways to vote.

Secure drop boxes are an option, and so is dropping off a completed ballot at a local polling place. And, as always, people can vote at their local polling place as long as they are in line by 8 p.m.

Some polling places in Salt Lake County will have federal monitors from the U.S. Department of Justice. We should find out today where they will be, and we have detailed what they can and can’t do.

You can find your closest voting location by searching by address on votesearch.utah.gov.

Utahns are allowed to return ballots for people they live with as long as each voter signs their own envelope.

For those who need it, some companies are offering the chance to take a discounted electric scooter, e-bike or rideshare to polling.

Note to readers • This blog will be updated throughout Election Day; check back for developing news.

It’s not easy to cut through all the noise of an election cycle.

Tribune journalists have you covered. We’ve spent hundreds of hours reaching out to candidates in more than 80 races. We’ve broken down ballot initiatives. We asked the questions you wanted candidates to answer, ensuring you know where they stand on affordability and water issues, among others.

All so you, and your neighbors, can make choices with confidence.

This work takes real resources to produce. As a nonprofit newsroom we can only do this with donations from readers like you.

Please make a gift today to ensure we can keep bringing you the information you need.

Treasury yields fell on Tuesday night, as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.

Actual Article Body:
Treasury yields fell  as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield dropped nearly 5 basis points to 4.902%. The 30-year bond yield slid 5.29%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield pulled back 6 basis points to 4.55%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.

Democrats are projected to win the House, according to a CNBC Election Desk projection. And while the Senate was still up for grabs, Democrats have already flipped a seat in North Carolina, with former Gov. Roy Cooper projected to win.

Stock futures fell sharply as election results rolled in. Contracts tied to to the S&P 500 shed 1.1%, and Nasdaq-100 futures slid 2%. AI-related shares, which have led the bull market, paced the overnight decline on fear Democrats would slow the data center buildout.

In Richmond, we've seen part of one precinct's vote in the Anne Holton-Jackie McDonnough school board race, and it's a big margin for McDonnough. There's just no way to extrapolate off those numbers, so it'll have to remain a curiosity for the moment.

Richmond's "Yes for RPS" campaign appears to be getting the job done, though. If we were in the prediction game, we'd be awfully close to making the call.

8:06 p.m. – Catch video updates from the newsroom all night long on Instagram at RichmonderNews

7:54 p.m. – An early surprise out of Chesterfield, which was considered likely to pass the 1% sales tax increase easily, as residents did with a bond referendum four years ago.

Unlike Richmond, the "no" vote has a strong early showing in Chesterfield. That said, keep in mind that we are only looking at day-of vote, and we have not seen any of the early vote yet, which is likely to be a larger overall number than the day-of vote.

There's still plenty of time for this number to swing, but as "yes" solidifies in Richmond, it's much more uncertain in Chesterfield.

7:28 p.m. – We've got our first two precincts reporting in Richmond, and it's good news for the "Yes for RPS" campaign, though there's still a ways to go.

These are both 1st District sites in the Near West End, where you'd expect cynicism about the 1% sales tax to be at its highest.

Still a long ways to go, but the very first indicator is positive for a potential sales tax increase.

5:50 p.m. – Polls close in a little more than one hour in Richmond, and turnout appears to be high on a beautiful day across the region.

Early voting numbers came in strong as well, with Chesterfield, Henrico and Richmond residents participating in early voting at 6-12% higher rates than they did in last year's elections.

Expect plenty more, as well as video updates and chats with voters, as we settle in at Richmonder HQ to document what promises to be an eventful night.

Today’s the day: Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. as Utah voters help decide on elected officials to represent them everywhere from their local county building to Washington, D.C.

(Abigail Landwehr  |  The Salt Lake Tribune) People wait in line to vote at Salt Lake City Public Library in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

Comment

Add as Preferred Source

Long lines across Utah are delaying election results. The state’s elections results website noted that lines are longer than 15 minutes and that “results will be delayed until lines are less than 15 minutes anywhere in the state, but no later than 9 p.m.”

At 8:07 p.m., there were a few hundred voters in line at the Cache County Event Center, but the line was moving steadily. County Clerk Bryson Behm estimated it would take about an hour to get everyone through.

Polls have closed in Utah’s elections, but if you’re in line you can still vote! Voters in line as of 8 p.m. have the right to cast a ballot.

Once all voters have cast their ballots, officials expect to start releasing early election results. Stay up to date on those races at sltrib.com/politics/election/

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

About 10 minutes before polls closed, about 50 people were in line outside the Salt Lake City Main Library, with more walking up to join the line.

Farther south, at the Draper Recreation Center, there were no lines to be seen with 10 minutes to go until 8 p.m.

In Utah County, voters lined up in their cars outside the American Fork Library to drop off their ballots.

Hours earlier in Cache County, voters were streaming through the county’s event center to cast their ballots.

Voter Douglas Goldman, who said his main priority was to keep government small, was frustrated at having to show his ID several times during the in-person voting process.

Roman Metivier, on the other hand, thought things were running smoothly. He had voted a few days earlier, but was at the center with several of his family members who were also there to cast ballots.

In St. George, voters faced lengthy lines at the Dixie Convention Center Tuesday evening, with some waiting over an hour to cast their ballot.

Crystal Hanza, who voted early, waited patiently in line with her two daughters who are students at Utah Tech University.

Despite the long lines, Roxy Hanza, 21, said the voting process went smoothly and she appreciated all the volunteers.

“Everyone was nice in there, and I think as a young person, it’s important that we go and vote,” she said.

She saw some of her classmates in line too, she added, and has seen young people posting about the election on social media.

Immigration and other social issues influenced the Hanzas’ votes this year.

She held up a rainbow charm on her necklace and told The Tribune she wore it in memory of Renee Good, who was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Minneapolis.

(Brooke Larsen | The Salt Lake Tribune) Voters stand in line at the Dixie Convention Center in St. George on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

“I do understand we need to have safe borders,” she added, “but I don’t think we need to be dehumanizing and ruthless about it.”

Jeremy Bradley told The Tribune he thought a lot of Washington County voters were turning out because of frustration with Utah judges. “I’ve had some friends say just vote no on all the judges, out with the old in with the new,” he said, “but I did not vote that way.”

For Navajo voters, Tuesday is a double Election Day.

“Not only do we have the county, state and federal races, we also have the Navajo Nation elections,” said Carma Claw, president of the Aneth Chapter in the Utah portion of the Navajo Nation.

Waves of floods have devastated the Navajo Nation and eroded dirt roads, cutting off access to polling locations for some. It’s why the state is allowing San Juan County residents to vote electronically.

But not all tribal members have internet access, Claw said, and the Navajo Nation doesn’t have an electronic voting option.

“Some are just saying they don’t have an ability to get here because of road closures,” Claw said. “There’s been a lot of areas in the community where the regular dirt roads are washed out completely.”

(Navajo Nation Division of Transportation) Heavy rains washed out Flat Top Mountain Road in Red Mesa, forcing a route closure on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, two days before Election Day.

Poll workers had to navigate eroded roads early Tuesday to setup voting centers, said Claw, who thanked poll workers, election staff and volunteers “for making voting even an option given this flood damage.”

Aneth Chapter members have to go two locations — 8 miles apart — to participate in both the U.S. election and Navajo Nation election. One voter told Claw they had to take a two-hour-long detour.

The San Juan River is expected to rise again Tuesday night, which could make the road between both locations “impassable,” Claw said.

Moving forward, the experience may inform organizers on how to better prepare for elections during natural disasters.

“This is a really important opportunity for people to voice their input, and a natural disaster should not be a part of why they can’t have that access,” Claw added.

Federal election monitors have stopped by at least half of Salt Lake County’s 40 voting centers, Chief Deputy Clerk Nikila Venugopal said Tuesday afternoon.

Turnout has remained steady throughout the day, Venugopal said, with voters quickly moving through the lines to drop off their ballots.

So far, neither Venugopal nor Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman were aware of any problems involving the federal monitors.

In Davis County, Clerk Brian McKenzie said Election Day voting had been “going really well,” with a steady stream of voters, both in-person and at drop boxes.

He expects that somewhere around 40-50% of voters — typical turnout for a midterm election — would cast ballots before polls close at 8 p.m.

Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman said federal election monitors sent by President Donald Trump’s Justice Department are visiting all 40 voting centers in the county Tuesday, spending about 30 minutes at each site.

By about noon, monitors had already hit several polling locations, including the Salt Lake County Government Center on State Street and Unified Fire Authority’s Fire Station 123 in Herriman, she said.

So far, Chapman said the monitors have followed state election laws and have not interacted with voters or disrupted the voting process.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune)  A voter at Draper Recreation Center on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

A spokesperson for Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson’s office also said Tuesday morning that they had not heard of any issues. The monitors were only expected in Salt Lake County.

Throughout the county, Salt Lake Tribune staff are seeing polling locations with steady but manageable lines.

At the Draper Recreation Center, at 657 E. Vestry Rd., polling staff said they saw long lines when it first opened at 7 a.m. — mostly from sweaty patrons looking to cast their vote after their morning workout. But by early afternoon, lines had shrunken considerably.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune)  Voting takes place in the Council Chambers at Draper City Hall on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

The estimated preelection turnout from Utah voters before polls opened throughout the state early Tuesday was 30%, Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson announced.

The highest turnout was in Grand County, with 60% estimated turnout, followed by Rich County with 58.8%.

In Utah County, where Clerk Aaron Davidson has said he is a proponent of in-person voting, preelection turnout was 19.3%, the second-lowest in the state. In Salt Lake County, the number hovered just under 34%.

On Tuesday morning, around 9 a.m., a steady stream of voters lined up at the ballot drop box outside the downtown Salt Lake City library — and found it nearly stuffed to the top. An elections division worker with the Salt Lake County clerk’s office noted someone was on the way to retrieve ballots as people continued to vote.

(Rachel Crosby | The Salt Lake Tribune) A driver votes across from City Hall in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

About 2.5 miles south, at the Salt Lake County Government Center, a Salt Lake Tribune reporter also noted cars queuing for the location’s drive-thru ballot drop box.

There were also plenty of residents walking inside to vote in-person.

Some San Juan County residents woke up to an email offering them an unusual option Tuesday, after flooding prompted Utah’s top election official to allow affected voters to cast their ballots electronically.

Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson declared emergency election accommodations Monday as record rainfall and flooding continued to disrupt the county, blocking roads and making it difficult for some residents to reach ballot drop boxes and polling locations.

“We want to make sure that every voter knows that they’re important, that their vote matters, and that if they wish to do so, they have every opportunity to cast their vote,” Henderson said at a news conference Monday.

San Juan County has about 6,000 registered voters, Henderson said, and the county clerk’s office has limited staff and is already “spread really thin.”

Unlocking the electronic option is a temporary emergency measure and will not change the state’s regular voting process in the future, she said.

The county sent an email Tuesday morning to voters who may need the accommodation and have an email address on file. Residents who have not voted and did not receive an email can contact the county clerk before 5 p.m. All electronic ballots must be submitted by 8 p.m.

County officials declared a local emergency Sunday, and Bluff Mayor Josh Ewing described the latest round of rain as “a one-two punch.”

Henderson, making her second visit to the county in a week, said Monday that roads and bridges had been washed away or submerged, while some homes and businesses were destroyed. Communities were just beginning to recover from last week’s flooding when more rain fell on already saturated ground over the weekend.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune) The voting location at Riverton City Hall on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

Today’s the day! Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. as Utah voters decide on who will represent them in offices everywhere from their local county government to Washington, D.C.

More than 1.7 million Utahns are registered to vote, according to Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson’s office.

Henderson, who oversees statewide elections, said about a third of voters had cast ballots as of Monday morning, with turnout ranging from 18% in San Juan County to more than 45% in Rich and Grand counties.

Three members of Utah’s House delegation are up for reelection, as U.S. Reps. Blake Moore, Celeste Maloy and Mike Kennedy look to win again in newly drawn congressional districts. U.S. Rep. Burgess Owens, who currently represents the state’s 4th Congressional District, is retiring, while former U.S. Rep. Ben McAdams is running again in the new 1st Congressional District.

Utahns also will vote for members of the state Legislature, two proposed congressional amendments, county councils, school boards and whether to retain judges.

Want to learn more about the races on your ballot? Check out The Tribune’s voter guides. Plug in your address and find guides for every race on your ballot.

In past elections, ballots postmarked on or by Election Day would be counted. But a change to Utah’s election laws now requires filled-out ballots to be in the hands of election officials or in an official drop box by 8 p.m. on election night to be counted.

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune)  Voting takes place at the Sandy Library on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

That means it’s far too late to mail your ballot, but there are still plenty of ways to vote.

Secure drop boxes are an option, and so is dropping off a completed ballot at a local polling place. And, as always, people can vote at their local polling place as long as they are in line by 8 p.m.

Some polling places in Salt Lake County will have federal monitors from the U.S. Department of Justice. We should find out today where they will be, and we have detailed what they can and can’t do.

You can find your closest voting location by searching by address on votesearch.utah.gov.

Utahns are allowed to return ballots for people they live with as long as each voter signs their own envelope.

For those who need it, some companies are offering the chance to take a discounted electric scooter, e-bike or rideshare to polling.

Treasury yields fell  as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield dropped nearly 5 basis points to 4.902%. The 30-year bond yield slid 5.29%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield pulled back 6 basis points to 4.55%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.

Democrats are projected to win the House, according to a CNBC Election Desk projection. And while the Senate was still up for grabs, Democrats have already flipped a seat in North Carolina, with former Gov. Roy Cooper projected to win.

Stock futures fell sharply as election results rolled in. Contracts tied to to the S&P 500 shed 1.1%, and Nasdaq-100 futures slid 2%. AI-related shares, which have led the bull market, paced the overnight decline on fear Democrats would slow the data center buildout.
